newsitem.title: USA: Fight grows over N.Y bond act, but voters favor it.
newsitem.headline: Fight grows over N.Y bond act, but voters favor it.

text.p: A battle over how New York State would spend $1.75 billion if a new green bond is approved heated up, as a lobbyist on Wednesday asked election officials to force an opponent to drop ads he said were false.
Despite the brouhaha, a new survey showed that New York's residents support the proposed environmental bond by 62 to 32 percent, according to a Quinnipiac College poll.

A fairly wide rift between upstate and downstate voters was revealed, however, as New York City residents back the act by a 73 to 15 percent margin, a much fatter lead than the 51 to 30 percent margin seen among upstate voters.

John Sheehan, a spokesman for the Adirondack Council, an environmental group that backs the act, asked the Board of Elections to stop another group from running ads saying "three out of four bond act dollars will go to New York City."

The ads were paid for by a group that calls itself "A Bunch of New Yorkers Who Like the Environment But Know This Bond Act is a Big Waste of Money." The Bunch includes two of the co-founders of the state's largest taxpayers' association, CHANGE-NY, which has criticized the bond act for not specifying precisely what projects will be funded.

A spokesman for CHANGE-NY said that the Bunch's advertisements were based on literature provided by a green group run by an official who is the co-chair of the political action committee that Gov. George Pataki set up to promote the bond act.
Pataki, who has worked hard to improve his standing on the environmental act by campaigning for its passage, helped organize a coalition of green groups to support the measure.

Paul Elston, who runs the New York League of Conservation Voters, is the co-chair of the political action committee for the bond act set up by Pataki. The other co-chair is Mike Finnegan, who is on leave from his role as the governor's chief counsel.
The League's education arm has put out literature saying that the city is eligible for up to $1.344 billion.

Tansie Whelan, a spokeswoman for the League, said that this estimate was correct, but added that last month it pulled the fact sheet cited by CHANGE-NY as it appeared to indicate New York City would get that total.
"The fact of the matter is that it's spread around," she said, referring to the division of the act's funds between upstate and downstate.

Gary Sheffer, the spokesman for bond act political action committee set up by Pataki, noted that all of New York's communities will have to compete for the bond act's funds. He added upstate communities and Long Island each are eligible for as much as New York City, adding that indeed each area could absorb the entire $1.75 billion, due to the magnitude of the projects delayed or never attempted.

In his filing, Sheehan said that only $225 million was specifically earmarked for environmental projects in New York City, while the act sets aside $325 million for upstate projects. He added almost $355 million from the act's Safe Drinking Program would go to upstate communities, while $230 million is earmarked for Long Island.
"Clearly, the majority of the Bond Act funds will benefit areas outside New York City," he wrote.
A spokesman for the Board of Elections, Lee Daghlian, noted that each complaint it gets, which must be filed by a citizen, is taken in order, a process that could take weeks or months.

Saying he doubted Sheehan's complaint, which he filed as a private citizen, could be acted upon before the November 5 polls, Daghlian added it might be quicker for Sheehan to take his fight to the courts. However, the lobbyist said that would be far too costly for him.
Sheehan said he was inspired to file his complaint in part by the narrow defeat in 1990 of the former Cuomo Administration's $1.98 billion environmental bond act, which he said lost by 70,000 votes.
